handoff.summary: Batch b01: five atomic biology records (three Hardy-Weinberg genotype-frequency predictions, allele-frequency-from-counts definition, population-density definition) grounded in OpenStax Biology 2e sections 19.1 and 45.1, each with two references, domain and missing-input rejections, and inverse notes. Two out-of-format/unverifiable discoveries deferred with exact sources.

assumptions: source assumption: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium conditions stated on the page: an infinitely large population with no mutations, migration, emigration, or selective pressure for or against genotype.

source assumption: exactly two alleles at one diploid locus with p + q = 1, and offspring genotypes formed by the random union of two gene-pool alleles (source: probability of obtaining genotypes 'if we draw two alleles at random from the gene pool').

gaps: Quantity meanings allele_frequency and genotype_frequency and dimensionless unit 1 for frequencies are not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot; runtime projection omitted.

models.inverse_notes: Allele frequency is recoverable as the nonnegative root of fAA (p = +sqrt(fAA)); the negative root is rejected by the p >= 0 guard. Substitution check: fAA = 0.64 gives p = 0.8, consistent with the violet-flower reference. Boundary p = 0 gives fAA = 0 (allele absent from the gene pool) and is admissible, not a violation. Joint inversion of (p, q) from fAA alone is underdetermined and not attempted.
limitations: Predicts the expected genotype frequency under equilibrium; a real population whose measured frequency deviates is evolving (drift, mutation, migration, selection).
Excludes loci with more than two alleles, sex linkage, polyploidy and nonrandom mating; the source notes no natural population fully satisfies the equilibrium conditions.

references.method: Published self-check answer: 320 VV of 500 plants (320/500 = 0.64) at p = 0.8; model answer verified on the CC-licensed practice mirror of section 19.1.
references.provenance: Published result (worked self-check with keyed model answer) converted from expected counts to frequency.

references.method: Figure 19.2 extended description: 245 YY of 500 individuals with allele frequency p = 0.7; 245/500 = 0.49 independently recomputed from the printed counts, matching the grid cell p-squared = .49.
references.provenance: Value derived independently from published figure counts (not the printed product).

rejection_cases.reason: Allele frequencies are bounded by 0 and 1; p = 1.2 is outside the frequency domain.

relationship.translation_notes: Superscript p-squared transcribed as p * p. Source symbols p (allele Y frequency) and pp (YY genotype frequency) preserved as local p and fAA. Dimensional check: dimensionless frequency times dimensionless frequency gives a dimensionless frequency. Independence of the two allele draws encodes the random-union assumption.

models.inverse_notes: Given fAa and nonzero p, q = fAa / (2p), symmetric in p and q. Substitution check: fAa = 0.32 with p = 0.8 gives q = 0.2, consistent with the violet-flower reference. The sum-to-one condition p + q = 1 is kept as an assumption, not an executable guard, to avoid floating-point equality on rounded published inputs.
limitations: Predicts the expected genotype frequency under equilibrium; a measured deviation means the population is evolving.
Excludes loci with more than two alleles, sex linkage, polyploidy and nonrandom mating.

assumptions: source assumption: diploid organisms in which each individual carries exactly two alleles per gene (source: 'Each individual in a population of diploid organisms can only carry two alleles for a particular gene').

models.inverse_notes: Total census size N is recoverable as (2*nAA + nAa) / (2*p) when p is nonzero; N = 0 is excluded by the guard because a frequency over an empty sample is undefined. Substitution check: 700 Y alleles at p = 0.7 give N = 700 / 1.4 = 500 individuals, consistent with the figure reference. Inverting for a single genotype count from p alone is underdetermined and not attempted.
limitations: Estimates the current gene-pool frequency from an observed census; it does not test equilibrium and must not be confused with the Hardy-Weinberg predicted frequencies, against which it is compared.
Requires complete, non-overlapping genotype classification; misclassified or unsampled individuals bias the frequency.

assumptions: source assumption: a population consists of all individuals of one particular species occurring in one particular area (source: population definition in section 45.1).

application profile: single-survey snapshot; the record describes the population at one point in time and carries no growth, dispersal or time-aggregation semantics (source: size and density 'describe a population at one particular point in time').

gaps: Quantity meanings individual_count, survey_area and population_density and count/area units are not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot; runtime projection omitted.

models.inverse_notes: Count is recoverable as N = D * A for nonzero area; A = 0 is excluded by the guard. Substitution check: D = 1.2 count/m2 over A = 100 m2 gives N = 120 individuals, consistent with the quadrat reference. Area is recoverable as A = N / D for nonzero density; the zero-density boundary leaves area undetermined, which is expected rather than a defect.
limitations: A single density number carries no information about spatial dispersion (uniform, random, clumped); the source stresses that dispersion must be measured separately.
Density alone does not estimate total population size without the corresponding total habitat area; quadrat samples require representative placement and sufficient replication.

references.method: Constructed quadrat-style check at the source's 100 m2 redwood-quadrat scale: 120 individuals in 100 m2 gives 1.2 per m2 by direct division; no field observation is claimed.
references.provenance: Independently constructed arithmetic check at a source-stated quadrat scale; not a published field value.

references.method: Admitted ideal boundary: an empty 1 m2 (daffodil-scale) quadrat holds zero individuals, giving zero density; verifies the N = 0 edge of the definition.
references.provenance: Definitional boundary check with an explicit ecological meaning (no individuals observed in the sampled area).

rejection_cases.reason: Density over zero area is undefined; a survey must state a positive sampled area.
Sampled area A is required; a bare count is population size, not density.

relationship.locator: Section 45.1 'Population Size and Density': N defined as 'the total number of individuals' and density as 'the number of individuals within a specific area or volume'; quadrat paragraph gives 1 m2 (daffodils) and 100 m2 (redwoods) as area-explicit sampling scales.
relationship.original_equation: population density = the number of individuals within a specific area or volume
relationship.translation_notes: Prose definition formalized as a ratio: the 'within a specific area' relation becomes division by the stated area. Source symbol N for population size preserved; D and A are introduced for density and area (the page names them only in prose). Dimensional check: count divided by area gives count per area. The glossary restatement 'number of population members divided by the area or volume being measured' (Lumen mirror of the same section) confirms the division reading.

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: a population is characterized by size N (total individuals) and density (individuals within a specific area or volume); quadrats of 1 m2 and 100 m2 illustrate area-explicit sampling.
